facts.statement: Siquisiquesuchus is an extinct genus of gavialid crocodilian named after the town of Siquisique in Lara, Venezuela, where the first specimens were found.
facts.quote: Siquisiquesuchus (meaning "Siquisique crocodile" after the town in Lara, Venezuela, near where the first described specimens were found) is an extinct genus of gavialid crocodilian.

facts.statement: Fossils of Siquisiquesuchus were found in Miocene-age rocks of the Castillo Formation in northwestern Venezuela.
facts.quote: It is known from cranial remains and a few postcranial bones found in Miocene-age rocks of the Castillo Formation in northwestern Venezuela.

facts.statement: The genus Siquisiquesuchus was described by Christopher Brochu and Ascanio Rincón in 2004.
facts.quote: These bones were described by Christopher Brochu and Ascanio Rincón in 2004.

facts.statement: The holotype of Siquisiquesuchus is specimen MBLUZ–P–5050, consisting of a nearly complete skull and lower jaws.
facts.quote: Siquisiquesuchus is based on the holotype MBLUZ–P–5050, a nearly complete skull and lower jaws.

facts.statement: Siquisiquesuchus had a long, narrow snout that made up approximately 60% of the total skull length.
facts.quote: Like other gavialoids, Siquisiquesuchus had a long, narrow rostrum on its skull, accounting for approximately 60% of the skull's length.

facts.statement: The upper jaw bones of Siquisiquesuchus held at least 20 teeth each, while the lower jaw bones held at least 23 teeth.
facts.quote: the maxillae making up most of the rostrum had at least 20 teeth each, and the dentaries of the lower jaws had at least 23.

facts.statement: Siquisiquesuchus fossils were found in marginal marine deposits, suggesting a coastal habitat.
facts.quote: Brochu and Rincón noted that Siquisiquesuchus was found in marginal marine deposits.

facts.statement: Researchers interpreted the presence of Siquisiquesuchus in South America as evidence that gavialoids dispersed across marine barriers to the Neotropics during the Tertiary period.
facts.quote: This, along with similarities to Old World gavialoids, was interpreted as evidence that gavialoids "dispersed across a marine barrier to the Neotropics during the Tertiary."

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the classification of Siquisiquesuchus; some researchers classify it as a gryposuchinae gavialid, while others have not assigned it to a specific family or subfamily.
facts.quote: Vélez–Juarbe and colleagues (2007) found it to be a gryposuchinae gavialid, while Jouve and colleagues (2008) did not assign families or subfamilies.

facts.statement: Siquisiquesuchus lived between 20.45 and 15.98 million years ago during the Burdigalian stage of the Miocene.
facts.quote: Time range: Burdigalian to Burdigalian (20.45 to 15.98 million years ago)

facts.statement: The genus Siquisiquesuchus is classified within the subfamily Gryposuchinae.
